title: The palace mourns
hookLine: Yasodhara's lament: why did he leave without me? (Buddhacarita 8)

cards: An empty saddle. That's what the city sees first. Kanthaka comes back through the gate with no rider, and Chandaka walks beside him holding a bundle of jewels.
People run into the streets, looking past the horse for the prince, and he isn't there. The horse has come home. The rider hasn't.
For a whole canto now, the poem leaves the hero in the forest and stays behind with everyone he left.

teach.b: First, the city. The poem fills the streets with weeping. Not long ago people watched the prince ride out in splendor.
Now the city feels like a house after a funeral. Second, the women of the palace, and Gautami, the queen who raised him after his mother died.
She grieves over small, precise things, the way people do: his long, beautiful hair, now cut and lying somewhere on the forest floor. Third, Yashodhara, his wife.
Her grief comes out as anger first, at Chandaka and even at the horse: why did you take him? Then it turns to the question underneath.

teach.h: WHY DID HE LEAVE WITHOUT ME?
teach.b: In paraphrase, she asks why he left without her. If he wanted the holy life, why not with her? She remembers the kings of old, his own ancestors in the stories, who went into the forest with their wives beside them.

He has gone to seek the highest good, she says, and left his partner behind, as if the good were something to be won alone. She isn't asking him to stay a prince. She's asking why she had no part in the leaving.

teach.h: THE KING FALLS TO THE GROUND.
teach.b: When Shuddhodana hears, the poem says, he falls to the ground in grief.
All his walls, all his music, and the son is gone anyway. A story like this could skip this part.

Ashvaghosha keeps the camera in the palace and lets the grief speak in full, without arguing with Yashodhara or hurrying her. The leaving was right for the prince, the poem believes, and it still cost someone.

how: Yashodhara is remembered in Buddhist tradition, and in later tellings she becomes a nun herself; her lament is part of how some Buddhists reflect on the cost of the prince's leaving to those who loved him.

o: the prince's mother, who dreamed of an elephant
the prince's wife, who asks why he left without her
the queen who raised the prince after Maya died

games.q: who mourns, and how: tap the pairs.
p: comes home with an empty saddle
asks why he left without her
falls to the ground in grief

s: in the poem, Yashodhara begs the prince to come back and rule
she asks why he left without her, not why he left the throne.
the poem stays in the palace for a whole canto after the leaving
it lets the grief of those left behind speak in full.
the poem scolds Yashodhara for her anger
it lets her speak without arguing back.

games.q: you're Yashodhara. the horse is home, the jewels are home, and your husband isn't. what do you do?
o: hide your grief and keep the palace calm.
speak your grief and your anger out loud.
set out after him into the forest.
games.why: she speaks, first in anger at Chandaka and the horse, then asking why he left without her, when kings of old went to the forest with their wives.

practice: Bring to mind someone left behind by a choice, maybe yours, a parent when you moved away, a friend when your life went a different way, or someone else's, and you were the one left.

Let that person be in the room, and say their name inside. You don't need to undo anything or decide who was right; just let their side of the story have its say, the way the poem lets Yashodhara speak.

wordCard.voice: Yashodhara. The prince's wife, who asks in the poem why he left for the holy life without her, as the whole palace grieves his going. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: the name of the prince's wife; Pali tellings often call her Yasodhara or Bimba.

carryVoice: Your line: the one left behind. The poem gives her grief room to speak. See you tomorrow.
